title: Read the error as a specific kernel error, not a generic failure
explanation: `webappctl start` fails with `Too many levels of symbolic links` — that's `ELOOP`, a distinct filesystem error from `ENOENT` (dangling symlink, nothing at the end) or `EACCES` (permission denied). It specifically means the kernel's path-resolution walk hit its symlink-hop limit (40 on Linux) without ever reaching a real file, which narrows the search to the symlink chain itself, not permissions or a missing config.

title: Inspect what the link's target text actually says
explanation: `readlink /etc/webapp/conf.active` shows the link points at `conf.active` — itself. `ls -l` alone would show "it's a symlink"; `readlink` is what reveals it's self-referential rather than pointing somewhere real, which is exactly the distinction that separates ELOOP from an ordinary broken link.

title: Confirm the real config was never actually touched
explanation: `cat /etc/webapp/profiles/prod/app.conf` shows a completely normal `LISTEN_PORT=8080` config, and `ls -l /etc/webapp/profiles/` confirms it's the only real profile on disk. A broken deploy script created the loop at the `conf.active` pointer — the actual profile data was never damaged.

title: Repoint the symlink at the real target
explanation: `sudo ln -sfn /etc/webapp/profiles/prod /etc/webapp/conf.active` replaces the self-referential link in one step. As with any symlink swap, `-n` matters here: without it, `ln` would try to follow `conf.active` (which loops) rather than replacing the link itself.

title: Verify the process actually started, not just that the read succeeded
explanation: `webappctl start` succeeding at reading the config is necessary but not sufficient — `pgrep -af webapp-worker` confirms the worker process it launches is genuinely running. `ELOOP` is enforced identically for root and unprivileged processes, so no amount of `sudo` would have resolved the loop without fixing the link itself.
